2.1 — Coins: Triggers, Tags & Your First Stat

Your character can walk, but it cannot touch anything. Walk straight over the coin and nothing happens — not because your code is wrong, but because nothing in this entire project is built to notice a collision. Today you make the first object in the game that reacts to the player, and in doing so you switch the physics engine on for good.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I detect a collision, and make something happen?”Full walkthrough
Break It Down~10 minFull walkthrough

Make a coin disappear when I touch it — "how do I detect a collision, and make something happen?" As one problem it is not even startable, because at this moment nothing in the whole project is built to notice that two objects touched.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give the coin a shape the engine can testA Circle Collider 2D on the prefab root, its radius dragged until the green outline covers the art, and Is Trigger ticked. Trigger matters: a solid collider shoves you back, a trigger only reports. Leave the collider on the root, because the root is the object carrying the Coin tag.Read: the Collider2D row in the quick reference, and the Is Trigger checkbox in the Inspector.
  2. Give the Player a shape and a bodyA Circle Collider 2D on the Player root — the root, not the Sprite child, because CompareTag is asked of whichever object owns the collider — plus a Rigidbody 2D with Body Type Dynamic, Gravity Scale 0 and Interpolate set. Two colliders with no body anywhere produce silence: no error, no warning, nothing to debug.Read: the Body Type warning in the quick reference — it is the first thing to check when nothing happens.
  3. Confirm the thing that triggered was a coinOnTriggerEnter2D runs on the first frame two shapes overlap, and its parameter is the other object's collider. The if (other.CompareTag("Coin")) check is what turns "something touched me" into "a coin touched me" — spikes, walls and cave doors all land in this same method before the unit is over.Read: the OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other) and other.CompareTag("Coin") rows in the quick reference.
  4. Change the countcoins = coins + 1; inside the check, with coins declared as a [SerializeField] private int back in the class body. No type in front of the line in the method: this assigns to a field that already exists, and declaring it here instead would rebuild it every frame and leave the real total at zero.Read: the [SerializeField] private float speed; row in the quick reference, and the declare-vs-assign rule you met in 1.3.
  5. Destroy the objectDestroy(other.gameObject); — other is a Collider2D, not a GameObject, so .gameObject walks up to the whole coin. Write Destroy(gameObject) by mistake and you delete the Player instead, which is the bug you will deliberately cause in the Bug Hunt.Read: the Destroy(gameObject) row in the quick reference, and the pickup pattern underneath it.

Three of these five parts are the pickup pattern in miniature — a check, a change, a destroy — and you will write them in that order all year. The first two are what this lesson is really about: Unity's rule is a collider on both objects and a body on at least one, and until it is satisfied the method never runs at all. That is why the split has to include the Inspector.

The test: when the coin does nothing, is there one part above you can point at and test on its own? A silent failure with no error in the Console is a physics problem, not a script problem — and a split that stops at the C# cannot tell you which.

Connect it to something you already built

Very little in this course is new. Most of it is something you have already done, pointed in a different direction — and saying which one out loud is how you stop relearning it every time.

Part three is the line that turns "something touched me" into "a coin touched me". In one sentence, say what the Player would do on the first frame it walked into a wall if that line were missing.

In 1.3 you learned that a value declared inside a method forgets itself between calls. Which part above is that rule deciding, and what would the coin count do if you got it wrong?

In 1.2 you read the Player as a Transform, an empty script, and a child Sprite. Which part above adds the first components to it since that day — and why does the collider have to sit on the root rather than on the Sprite?

In 1.6 you cached the Animator with GetComponentInChildren because the component lived on the child. Today part three checks a tag. What is that check actually asked of — the picture you can see, or the object that owns the collider?

The Problem ~10 min

Your goal: make a coin disappear when the player touches it. Before you write a single line, answer this honestly — how would Unity ever know the two objects touched? The Player has a Transform. The Coin has a Transform. Two positions in space do not collide. Nothing in the engine is checking.

Something has to tell it what shape each object is, and something has to be simulated every frame so those shapes can be tested against each other. Read what Unity gives you:

ComponentWhat it contributes
Collider2D Gives an object a shape the physics engine can test against other shapes. Without one, an object is invisible to physics — it is only a picture.
Rigidbody2D Puts an object under simulation: the engine tracks it every physics step, and it is what makes overlap messages fire at all.
Is Trigger (checkbox on any Collider2D) Changes what an overlap means. A solid collider pushes objects apart. A trigger does not push — it only reports that the overlap happened.
OnTriggerEnter2D The message your script receives on the first frame two shapes overlap. This is the event a coin pickup is built on.
CompareTag How you check what you just touched. Asks the engine whether a collider carries a given tag.
The rule that catches everyone. Unity's 2D physics only simulates objects that have a Collider2D, and overlap messages only fire when at least one of the two objects also has a Rigidbody2D. Two colliders with no body anywhere produce silence — no error, no warning, nothing to debug.

And here is the part that matters today: in this project nothing in Assets/Prefabs has either one — except the Switch. Not the Player. Not the Coin. Not the Spikes. You are about to be the first person to give anything in this game a physics body.

Socratic: What Is a Collider For?

  1. A Transform stores position, rotation and scale. What does a Collider2D store that a Transform has no way to express?
  2. The physics engine runs on its own schedule, not inside your Update(). Why would Unity be built that way, instead of letting your script test for overlaps once a frame?
  3. A trigger pushes nothing — it only reports. Name two game behaviours besides a coin pickup where a report-only overlap is the right tool.
  4. A collider is a shape; a rigidbody is a thing under simulation. The Player is the object that moves. Which of the two must live on the Player for a coin to ever notice it, and which one could live on the coin instead?
  5. The minimum is "a collider on both, a body on one". Which object should carry the body — the coin that sits still and vanishes, or the player that moves all game? Argue it, then build it that way.
Build It With MeFull walkthrough

The question this answers“how do I make a coin disappear when I touch it?”

You are editing Assets/Prefabs/Coin and Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. Two objects to wire up in the Inspector, then one method on the Player. Every setting and every line is given below.

Step 1Give the Coin a shape

A coin is currently a picture and nothing else. Start by giving it a shape the physics engine can test.

1Hierarchy or Project ▸ select the Coin prefab2Coin (root) ▸ Add Component ▸ Circle Collider 2D3Circle Collider 2D ▸ Radius   →  drag to fit the coin4Circle Collider 2D ▸ Is Trigger   ☑ ON
  1. 1Work on the prefab asset in Assets/Prefabs, not one instance in the scene. Anything you change on the prefab applies to every coin you ever place.
  2. 2This is the coin's shape. Before this, the engine has no idea the coin occupies any space at all.A Circle is the right shape here because the coin is round. Unity also offers Box, Capsule, Polygon and Edge — pick the one that matches the silhouette, because a bad shape means a coin you can collect by touching empty air.
  3. 3Check the green outline in the Scene view. Does it cover the coin you can actually see?Two things to get right here. The size: a new collider does not fit itself to your art, so drag the radius until the green outline covers the coin. The place: leave the collider on the root, because the root is the object carrying the Coin tag. Move it down to the Untagged Sprite child and CompareTag("Coin") becomes false, and the pickup silently does nothing.
  4. 4Tick it. This changes what an overlap means: a solid collider shoves objects apart, a trigger does not push at all — it only reports that the overlap happened.Leave this off and the coin behaves like a wall. You still get a message, but you also get stopped dead in your tracks — which is a bug you can feel immediately.

Step 2Give the Player a shape AND a body

A collider alone is not enough. Unity's rule: colliders on both objects, a Rigidbody2D on at least one.

1Assets/Prefabs/Player (root) ▸ Add Component ▸ Circle Collider 2D2Assets/Prefabs/Player (root) ▸ Add Component ▸ Rigidbody 2D3Rigidbody 2D ▸ Body Type       =  Dynamic4Rigidbody 2D ▸ Gravity Scale   =  05Rigidbody 2D ▸ Interpolate     =  Interpolate6( Constraints are still empty for now — see the note below. )
  1. 1The Player's shape. Add it to the root, then drag the radius until the green outline fits the character you can see.The root, not the Sprite child, and this is not a style preference. The cave-entrance script checks collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Player"), and collision.gameObject is whichever object owns the collider. Put the collider on the Untagged Sprite child and the cave door never opens for you — with no error to explain why.
  2. 2The body. This puts the Player under simulation, and it is what makes overlap messages fire at all.This is the component everyone forgets. Two colliders with no body anywhere produce total silence — no error, no warning, no message, nothing to debug. If your coin does nothing at all later, come back to this line first.
  3. 3A Dynamic body is simulated: it collides, and it can be pushed. This is what you want for a character that gets knocked back later.Keep it Dynamic. You are still Dynamic at the end of the year, including in the cave where gravity matters. Notice what you just chose: Dynamic is the body type that actually collides. Right now nothing in the world is solid to you — in 2.2 you make the spikes solid, and this is the setting that decides whether you stop at them.
  4. 4Set it to 0. Your world is seen from directly above and has no "down" for anything to fall toward.The default is 1. Leave it and your character immediately starts sliding off the bottom of the screen the moment you press Play. This is the single most common surprise in this lesson.
  5. 5Smooths the rendered position between physics steps. Physics runs on its own clock, and without this your movement looks slightly jerky.
  6. 6A Dynamic body picks up spin when something solid hits it off-centre. There is almost nothing solid to you yet, so you leave this alone today and deal with it properly in 2.2.One exception, and you may meet it in this lesson: the cave entrances are solid. If your character tumbles after touching one, that is a Dynamic body picking up torque — not a broken script. You will freeze the rotation in 2.2, next lesson.

Step 3Write the pickup on the Player

One new field and one new method on PlayerController. The Player is what moves, so the Player is what gets told about the overlap.

1    [SerializeField] private int coins;23    private void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)4    {5        if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))6        {7            coins = coins + 1;8            Debug.Log("Coins collected: " + coins);9            Destroy(other.gameObject);10        }11    }
  1. 1How many coins you have collected. An int (whole number), exposed to the Inspector so you can watch it change while the game runs.Declared in the class body, not inside the method — the same rule from 1.3. This is state that has to still be there on the next frame, so it belongs to the object.
  2. 3Unity calls this on the first frame two shapes overlap. You do not call it yourself. The parameter is the *other* object's collider — the one that ran into you.
  3. 5Check what you just touched before doing anything. CompareTag asks the engine directly; comparing tag strings with == builds a new string every call and can silently miss.Spikes, cave entrances and healing pickups will all land in this same method before the unit is over. Without this check, the Player would vanish the first time it walked into a wall that happened to have a collider.
  4. 7Add one to the running total. Notice there is no type in front — coins already exists, so this assigns to it. Writing int coins = coins + 1; here would create a brand-new local that dies at the end of the frame and leave the real total frozen at zero.
  5. 8Print the new total. With no UI in this game yet, the Console is the only way to see the number go up.
  6. 9Removes the coin. other is a Collider2D, not a GameObject — .gameObject walks up from the collider to the whole object it belongs to.other.gameObject — not gameObject. Using plain gameObject destroys the Player, which is the bug you will deliberately cause in the Bug Hunt below. Get it backwards and the game is instantly unplayable.
  7. 11Closes the method. The tag check exists so the destroy only ever reaches a coin.

Where this goes wrong

These are the mistakes this step actually produces. Read them before you are surprised by one.

  • Colliders on both objects, but no Rigidbody2D anywhere

    You will seeAbsolutely nothing happens. No error, no Console message, no warning. The coin sits there and the game looks fine.

    Do thisAt least one of the two objects needs a Rigidbody2D. Put it on the Player, since the Player is the thing that moves.

  • leaving Gravity Scale at its default of 1 on the Player

    You will seeThe character slides off the bottom of the screen the instant you press Play, and you cannot walk back.

    Do thisGravity Scale = 0. A top-down world has no down.

  • Destroy(gameObject) instead of Destroy(other.gameObject)

    You will seeYou collect one coin and the Player disappears instead. The camera goes dead.

    Do thisother is the thing you collided with. other.gameObject is it. Plain gameObject is you.

  • forgetting to tick Is Trigger on the coin

    You will seeOnTriggerEnter2D never runs, and the coin stops you dead like a wall.

    Do thisIs Trigger ☑ ON. A solid collider reports a *collision* (OnCollisionEnter2D), not a trigger.

  • the collider added to the Sprite child instead of the root

    You will seeCoins still work, but the cave entrance never opens. Nothing in the Console either way, so there is no clue to follow.

    Do thisThe collider belongs on the root — the object that carries the tag. CompareTag is asked of whichever GameObject owns the collider, and the Sprite child is Untagged.

  • a collider radius that was never fitted to the sprite

    You will seeYou collect coins by touching empty air a character-width away, or you have to stand in exactly one spot for it to register.

    Do thisSelect the collider and drag its Radius until the green outline in the Scene view matches what you can see. A new collider does not size itself to your art.

  • the coin's tag left as Untagged

    You will seeThe overlap fires, the coin stays put, and no message appears. The if was false.

    Do thisThe prefab ships with the tag Coin already set. If you changed it, set it back — and remember a tag change on a scene instance can be overwritten by the prefab on save.

Check your work: the finished file

Compare against your own file and Inspector. The two things to check hardest: that coins is declared in the class body rather than inside the method, and that the destroy says other.gameObject.

// Added to Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs, alongside your movement code.
// The fields all sit together in the class body; the method sits below Update().

    [SerializeField] private int coins;

    private void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
    {
        if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))
        {
            coins = coins + 1;
            Debug.Log("Coins collected: " + coins);
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
        }
    }

// Inspector changes made in this lesson:
//   Assets/Prefabs/Coin      : + Circle Collider 2D (Is Trigger ON, radius fitted)
//   Assets/Prefabs/Player    : + Circle Collider 2D on the ROOT (radius fitted)
//                              + Rigidbody 2D  (Dynamic, Gravity Scale 0,
//                                               Interpolate)
//                              Constraints left empty on purpose — 2.2 sets
//                              Freeze Rotation Z once things are solid.
What You Just Switched On ~10 min
A body changes the whole game — go and see what you broke. The moment the Player has a Collider2D and a Rigidbody2D, every collider in the scene starts interacting with it. That includes the Cave Entrances, which carry solid colliders wired to a scene-switching script that has been sitting dormant this whole time, precisely because your Player had no collider to trip it.

So: walk into a cave mouth and find out what happens. If you are suddenly standing in a different scene, nothing is broken — you switched the physics engine on. Write down what happened and why. Do not fix it yet, and do not delete the cave entrances: Unit 5 builds the cave properly, and this is the first thread of it.
One number, one home. For now the coin count lives on PlayerController. There is a StatManager.cs in Assets/Scripts — it is empty, and it stays empty. Later in the year you will have a real reason to move your stats into a manager, and that reason will come from a scene change, not from tidiness. Until then, every stat you build belongs to the player.
Read the Docs: Where Should a Stat Live? ~10 min

You just made a real design decision without being told to. Here are the three honest options for where a number like "coins" can live, and what each one costs:

ApproachWhat it looks likeWhat it costsWhen it wins
(a) A field on PlayerController [SerializeField] private int coins; The player owns the number, so anything else that wants it must find the player first. Now. The only thing that touches coins is the player.
(b) A separate PlayerStats component The numbers live in a component whose only job is numbers. One more component, one more reference to cache, one more thing to keep in sync. When PlayerController grows long enough that movement code and stat code start fighting over the same file.
(c) A global singleton StatManager Any script, anywhere, reads the numbers from one shared object. Everything can reach it, so nothing protects it — and to be worth having at all, it must survive a scene change. When several systems need the same numbers and those numbers must outlive a scene load.

Where Does a Number Belong?

  1. Which of the three did you just build, and which line of your own code proves it?
  2. Open Assets/Scripts/StatManager.cs and read it. If you filled it in as a singleton today, would your coin count survive a scene change? Would that be a feature or a problem right now?
  3. The coin disappears when collected, but "how many coins I have" is not a property of the coin. So where does that number really belong — the object that vanishes, or the object that persists?
  4. Which option makes the number easiest to find when you reopen this project in three weeks, and which makes it easiest to test on its own?
  5. You just watched a cave entrance teleport you somewhere. What does that tell you about whether your stats need to survive a scene change this month?
Bug Hunt & Tinker ~25 min

Bug Hunt: Tracing Pickup Bugs

  1. Untick Is Trigger on the coin's collider. Does OnTriggerEnter2D still run? What happens instead, and where does the player end up?
  2. Remove the Rigidbody2D from the Player but leave every collider in place. Does the coin still vanish? Does the Console show a message, or nothing at all?
  3. Change your destroy call to Destroy(gameObject) and collect a coin. Which object disappeared — and what is the Console still printing that tells you the player survived?
  4. Comment out the destroy line and walk in and out of the same coin five times. What does the count say? Why is a coin that pays out every time a bug rather than a bonus?
  5. Set the Player's Gravity Scale back to 1. What does the character do when you stop pressing keys, and which setting was quietly doing the work all along?
  6. Move your coins = coins + 1; line up so it sits before the if check instead of inside it. Walk into a wall. What does the count do, and what does that tell you about what the if is actually guarding?
  7. Walk into a Cave Entrance deliberately with your new body and collider. Which two components you added are responsible — and given the tag check inside that script, why did it react to you and not to a wall?

Tinker: Destroy versus SetActive

  1. Replace Destroy(other.gameObject) with other.gameObject.SetActive(false). What changes on screen, what is different in the Hierarchy after you stop playing, and what happens to your count?
  2. Read the docs for SetActive. In a game with thousands of coins, why might switching an object off and reusing it beat destroying it and building a new one?
  3. Open Assets/Scripts/Package Scripts/SceneSwitch.cs and find the method that fires when the player touches a cave mouth. Which parameter type does it take, and which of the two components you added today made it fire?
  4. Print your coin count with Debug.Log every frame instead of only on pickup. What happens to the Console, and why was printing on the event the better choice?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain what a Collider2D is for, and what a Rigidbody2D adds on top of it
  • State the rule — colliders on both, a body on at least one — and say which object you gave the body to, and why
  • Explain trigger versus solid, and defend the coin's choice
  • Explain what the parameter in OnTriggerEnter2D actually refers to, and why CompareTag beats comparing tag strings
  • Point at your own file and say why coins is declared in the class body while coins = coins + 1; is not
  • State where the coin count lives, and name one alternative you rejected, with a reason
  • Explain what happened at the cave entrance, and why it is not a bug
  • Commit and push
